before.content_html:
Chemical Symbols and Formulae

Every element has a unique chemical symbol, shown on the periodic table. Compounds are represented by chemical formulae that show which elements are present and how many atoms of each. For example, \(H_2O\) tells you water contains 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom. \(CaCO_3\) tells you calcium carbonate contains 1 calcium, 1 carbon and 3 oxygen atoms. Small subscript numbers apply to the element directly before them; a number before a formula (a coefficient) multiplies every atom in that formula.

Working out the formula of a compound from its name requires knowledge of ion charges. For example, sodium chloride is \(NaCl\) because \(Na^+\) and \(Cl^-\) balance in a 1:1 ratio. Magnesium oxide is \(MgO\) (\(Mg^{2+}\) and \(O^{2-}\)).

Key Fact

Chemical formulae show which elements are present and the ratio of atoms. Subscript numbers apply to the preceding element; coefficients multiply the whole formula. \(H_2O\) = 2 hydrogen + 1 oxygen.

Writing and Balancing Equations

A chemical equation shows reactants on the left and products on the right, separated by an arrow (\(\rightarrow\)). A word equation uses names: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide. A symbol equation uses formulae: \(2Mg + O_2 \rightarrow 2MgO\).

Symbol equations must be balanced so that the number of atoms of each element is the same on both sides. This reflects the conservation of mass — atoms are rearranged in reactions but never created or destroyed (C3.1a). To balance an equation: count atoms on each side, add coefficients (large numbers in front of formulae) until both sides match, and never change the subscript numbers in a formula.

Balance the reaction between hydrogen and oxygen to form water:

Unbalanced: \(H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow H_2O\)

Count atoms: Left — 2 H, 2 O. Right — 2 H, 1 O. Oxygen is unbalanced.

Put a 2 in front of \(H_2O\): \(H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O\). Now right side has 4 H and 2 O. Left has 2 H and 2 O. Hydrogen is unbalanced.

Put a 2 in front of \(H_2\): \(2H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O\). Now both sides have 4 H and 2 O. Balanced.

Key Fact

Equations must be balanced: same number of atoms on each side. Add coefficients to balance — never change subscript numbers. Conservation of mass: total mass of reactants = total mass of products.

State Symbols

State symbols are written after each formula to show the physical state: (s) = solid, (l) = liquid, (g) = gas, (aq) = aqueous (dissolved in water). For example:

$$2Na(s) + 2H_2O(l) \rightarrow 2NaOH(aq) + H_2(g)$$

State symbols give extra information about reaction conditions and help you understand whether substances are dissolved, gaseous, etc.

Conservation of mass can be demonstrated experimentally. If you carry out a reaction in a sealed container and measure the total mass before and after, it remains the same. In open containers, reactions that produce gas may appear to lose mass (because the gas escapes), but the total mass of all products — including the gas — equals the total mass of reactants.

An important application of balanced equations is calculating reacting masses. Using relative atomic masses from the periodic table, you can work out how much product will form from a given amount of reactant. For example, from \(2Mg + O_2 \rightarrow 2MgO\): 2 moles of magnesium (48 g) react with 1 mole of oxygen (32 g) to form 2 moles of magnesium oxide (80 g). This confirms conservation of mass: 48 + 32 = 80.

You should also be aware of the difference between exothermic reactions (which release energy to the surroundings, causing a temperature rise, e.g. combustion and neutralisation) and endothermic reactions (which absorb energy from the surroundings, causing a temperature drop, e.g. thermal decomposition and dissolving ammonium nitrate in water). Energy changes during reactions are linked to the breaking and forming of chemical bonds.

Breaking bonds requires energy (endothermic process), while forming bonds releases energy (exothermic process). In an exothermic reaction, the energy released by forming new bonds exceeds the energy needed to break existing bonds, so the overall reaction releases energy to the surroundings and the temperature rises. In an endothermic reaction, the opposite is true — more energy is needed to break bonds than is released when new bonds form.

Types of Chemical Reaction

OCR Gateway requires knowledge of several reaction types (C3.1b):

• Combustion: a substance reacts with oxygen, releasing energy. \(CH_4 + 2O_2 \rightarrow CO_2 + 2H_2O\)
• Displacement: a more reactive element replaces a less reactive one. \(Zn + CuSO_4 \rightarrow ZnSO_4 + Cu\)
• Neutralisation: acid + base → salt + water. \(HCl + NaOH \rightarrow NaCl + H_2O\)
• Oxidation: gaining oxygen (or losing electrons). Reduction: losing oxygen (or gaining electrons). Redox reactions involve both.
• Thermal decomposition: a substance breaks down when heated. \(CaCO_3 \rightarrow CaO + CO_2\)

Key Fact

Key reaction types: combustion (fuel + oxygen), displacement (reactive metal replaces less reactive one), neutralisation (acid + base → salt + water), thermal decomposition (breaks down with heat). All must be balanced.

before.content_html:
Energy Changes in Reactions

Every chemical reaction involves an energy change. Energy is either transferred to the surroundings or absorbed from them. The key principle is that energy is transferred, never created or destroyed. Two categories describe the direction of energy transfer. Understanding these categories — and the bond-level explanation for why energy is transferred — is fundamental to the whole of chemistry. Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between the system and the surroundings.

Key Fact

Exothermic reactions transfer energy to the surroundings — the temperature of the surroundings increases. Endothermic reactions take in energy from the surroundings — the temperature of the surroundings decreases.

Exothermic reactions include combustion (burning fuels), neutralisation (acid + alkali), and many oxidation reactions. Everyday examples include hand warmers (the crystallisation of a supersaturated sodium acetate solution) and self-heating food cans. Endothermic reactions include thermal decomposition, the reaction of citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate, thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate, and photosynthesis. Sports cold packs are a practical example — the endothermic dissolution of ammonium nitrate in water absorbs heat, cooling the injured area.

Measuring Energy Changes (PAG C5)

You can identify whether a reaction is exothermic or endothermic by measuring the temperature change of the surroundings (usually a solution in a polystyrene cup). If the temperature rises, the reaction is exothermic. If the temperature falls, the reaction is endothermic. A polystyrene cup is used as an insulator to reduce heat loss to the surroundings, giving a more accurate temperature reading. You should record the starting temperature, the maximum (or minimum) temperature, and calculate the change. In a well-insulated system, a bigger temperature change indicates a more energetic reaction.

Reaction Profiles

A reaction profile is a diagram that shows the energy levels of the reactants and products, and the energy change during a reaction. On the vertical axis is energy; on the horizontal axis is the progress of the reaction (sometimes labelled “reaction pathway”). The diagram does not show time — it simply shows the energy changes as reactants transform into products.

For an exothermic reaction, the products are at a lower energy level than the reactants — the energy difference has been released to the surroundings. The profile shows a “hump” from reactants rising to a peak (the activation energy barrier) then falling to a lower product level. For an endothermic reaction, the products are at a higher energy level than the reactants — energy has been absorbed. The profile shows a hump rising to the peak then settling at a level higher than the starting point. In both cases, the hump represents the activation energy — the minimum energy needed for the reaction to start. You must label four things on any reaction profile: the energy level of reactants, the energy level of products, the activation energy (from reactants to the peak), and the overall energy change (from reactants to products).

Key Fact

Activation energy is the minimum energy that colliding particles need for a reaction to occur. It is shown on a reaction profile as the difference between the reactant energy level and the top of the energy barrier (the peak).

Bond Energy Calculations (Higher)

During a chemical reaction, bonds in the reactants must be broken (this requires energy — endothermic) and new bonds in the products are made (this releases energy — exothermic). The overall energy change depends on the balance between these two processes. This is a Higher Tier calculation that requires you to use given bond energy values:

Step 1: Add up the total energy needed to break all the bonds in the reactants. Step 2: Add up the total energy released when all the bonds in the products are formed. Step 3: Calculate the overall energy change:

$$\text{energy change} = \text{energy to break bonds} - \text{energy released making bonds}$$

If the answer is positive, the reaction is endothermic (more energy needed to break bonds than is released making them). If the answer is negative, the reaction is exothermic (more energy released making bonds than needed to break them).

For example, for \(H_2 + Cl_2 \rightarrow 2HCl\): breaking bonds = H–H (436 kJ) + Cl–Cl (242 kJ) = 678 kJ. Making bonds = 2 × H–Cl (431 kJ) = 862 kJ. Energy change = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ. Negative, so exothermic. More energy was released making the H–Cl bonds than was required to break the H–H and Cl–Cl bonds, so the surplus energy is transferred to the surroundings as heat. This is why the overall reaction is exothermic. Remember: you must always consider all bonds broken and all bonds made, not just some of them.

Key Fact

Breaking bonds requires energy (endothermic). Making bonds releases energy (exothermic). If more energy is released making bonds than absorbed breaking them, the reaction is exothermic overall.

• If more energy is released making new bonds than breaking old ones, the reaction is exothermic overall.
• The overall energy change = energy to break bonds – energy released making bonds.

before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Exothermic reactions release energy (temperature rises); endothermic reactions absorb energy (temperature falls).
  • Reaction profiles show energy levels of reactants and products, the activation energy barrier, and whether the overall change is exothermic or endothermic.
  • Bond energy calculations: overall energy change = energy to break bonds − energy released making bonds. Negative = exothermic, positive = endothermic.

before.content_html:
Oxidation and Reduction

Oxidation is the gain of oxygen or the loss of electrons. Reduction is the loss of oxygen or the gain of electrons. These always happen together in what are called redox reactions. A useful mnemonic is OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss (of electrons), Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).

For example, when copper oxide is reduced by carbon: \(2CuO + C \rightarrow 2Cu + CO_2\). The copper oxide loses oxygen (it is reduced) and the carbon gains oxygen (it is oxidised). Carbon is the reducing agent (it causes the reduction of copper oxide) and copper oxide is the oxidising agent (it causes the oxidation of carbon). At Higher Tier, you also need to explain redox in terms of electrons: the substance that is oxidised loses electrons, and the substance that is reduced gains electrons. For example, in the formation of magnesium oxide: \(Mg \rightarrow Mg^{2+} + 2e^-\) (oxidation) and \(O + 2e^- \rightarrow O^{2-}\) (reduction).

Key Fact

Oxidation = gain of oxygen OR loss of electrons. Reduction = loss of oxygen OR gain of electrons. In terms of electrons (Higher): the substance that is oxidised loses electrons; the substance that is reduced gains electrons.

Acids and Alkalis

Acids produce hydrogen ions (\(H^+\)) when they dissolve in water. Solutions of alkalis contain hydroxide ions (\(OH^-\)). The pH scale measures how acidic or alkaline a solution is, running from 0 (very strong acid) to 14 (very strong alkali). pH 7 is neutral, below 7 is acidic, and above 7 is alkaline. Each step on the pH scale represents a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration.

You can measure pH using universal indicator (which changes colour across a range: red for strong acids, green for neutral, purple for strong alkalis) or a pH meter (which gives a precise numerical reading). Litmus paper gives a simple acid/alkali test but cannot distinguish between different strengths.

Dilute and concentrated refer to the amount of acid dissolved in a given volume of water. Strong and weak refer to the degree of ionisation. A strong acid (e.g. hydrochloric acid) fully ionises in water — every molecule produces \(H^+\) ions. A weak acid (e.g. ethanoic acid) only partially ionises — only some molecules produce \(H^+\) ions. When the hydrogen ion concentration increases by a factor of ten, the pH decreases by one.

Neutralisation and Making Salts

Neutralisation occurs when an acid reacts with a base or alkali to form a salt plus water. The ionic equation for neutralisation is:

$$H^+(aq) + OH^-(aq) \rightarrow H_2O(l)$$

Key reactions to know:

Acid + metal \(\rightarrow\) salt + hydrogen. For example: \(Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) \rightarrow MgCl_2(aq) + H_2(g)\).

Acid + metal carbonate \(\rightarrow\) salt + water + carbon dioxide. For example: \(CaCO_3(s) + 2HCl(aq) \rightarrow CaCl_2(aq) + H_2O(l) + CO_2(g)\).

Acid + alkali \(\rightarrow\) salt + water. For example: \(NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) \rightarrow NaCl(aq) + H_2O(l)\).

Key Fact

The name of the salt depends on the acid used: hydrochloric acid \(\rightarrow\) chloride salts, sulfuric acid \(\rightarrow\) sulfate salts, nitric acid \(\rightarrow\) nitrate salts.

Electrolysis

Electrolysis is the process of using an electric current to decompose (break down) an ionic compound that is either molten or dissolved in water. The ionic compound must be in a liquid state (molten or dissolved in water) so that the ions are free to move and carry the electrical current. Solid ionic compounds cannot be electrolysed because their ions are held in fixed positions within the lattice.

The ionic compound is placed in a container with two electrodes connected to a power supply. Positive ions (cations) move towards the cathode (negative electrode), where they gain electrons and are reduced. Negative ions (anions) move towards the anode (positive electrode), where they lose electrons and are oxidised. Metals (or hydrogen) form at the cathode; non-metals form at the anode.

For molten binary compounds, predicting products is straightforward. For example, molten sodium chloride produces sodium at the cathode and chlorine at the anode. For aqueous solutions, there are competing reactions because water also contains \(H^+\) and \(OH^-\) ions. At the cathode, hydrogen is produced instead of the metal if the metal is more reactive than hydrogen. At the anode, oxygen is usually produced (from \(OH^-\) ions) unless halide ions are present, in which case the halogen is produced. For example, electrolysing aqueous copper sulfate with inert (carbon) electrodes produces copper at the cathode (because copper is less reactive than hydrogen) and oxygen at the anode (because no halide ions are present). The electrodes used matter: inert electrodes (such as carbon or platinum) do not take part in the reaction, whereas non-inert electrodes (such as copper) can themselves dissolve or be deposited during electrolysis.

Key Fact

At the cathode: \(\text{Na}^+ + e^- \rightarrow \text{Na}\) (reduction). At the anode: \(2\text{Cl}^- \rightarrow Cl_2 + 2e^-\) (oxidation). Half equations show what happens at each electrode separately.
before.exam_tip_html: For electrolysis questions, always identify whether the compound is molten or aqueous — this changes the products. Write half equations for each electrode and state whether oxidation or reduction occurs. For acid reactions, be systematic: identify the acid, the base/metal/carbonate, and then predict the salt name. Show balanced equations with state symbols where possible.

practice_questions.text: State the name of the product formed at the cathode during the electrolysis of molten lead bromide.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark:
• Lead (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens to the ions during the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Na⁺ ions move to the cathode / negative electrode and gain electrons to form sodium (1).
• Cl⁻ ions move to the anode / positive electrode and lose electrons to form chlorine (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain, in terms of electron transfer, why the reaction \(2Mg + O_2 \rightarrow 2MgO\) is a redox reaction.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Magnesium loses electrons / is oxidised (1).
• Oxygen gains electrons / is reduced (1).
• Both oxidation and reduction occur in the same reaction, so it is redox (1).

practice_questions.text: A student adds excess zinc to a beaker of copper sulfate solution. The solution changes from blue to colourless and a brown solid forms. Compare the reactivity of zinc and copper, and suggest what type of reaction has occurred.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Zinc is more reactive than copper (1).
• Zinc displaces copper from the solution (1).
• This is a displacement / redox reaction (1).
• Zinc is oxidised (loses electrons), copper ions are reduced (gain electrons) (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe how to make a pure, dry sample of copper chloride crystals from copper oxide and hydrochloric acid.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Add excess copper oxide to warm hydrochloric acid and stir / filter off excess solid (1).
• Gently heat the filtrate to evaporate some water, then leave to crystallise (1).

practice_questions.text: Aqueous copper sulfate solution is electrolysed using inert (carbon) electrodes. Discuss what products form at each electrode and explain why these products form rather than alternatives. Include half equations in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Top band (5-6): Correct products at each electrode with explanations referencing competing ions, correct half equations, and clear reasoning.
Mid band (3-4): Identifies products with some explanation or partial half equations.
Lower band (1-2): Names one or both products with limited explanation.
Indicative content:
• Cathode: copper is deposited (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu) because copper is less reactive than hydrogen.
• Anode: oxygen gas is produced (4OH⁻ → 2H₂O + O₂ + 4e⁻) because sulfate ions are not discharged / OH⁻ ions from water are discharged preferentially (no halide ions present).
• The solution contains Cu²⁺, SO₄²⁻, H⁺ and OH⁻ ions.
• At the cathode, Cu²⁺ is preferentially discharged because Cu is less reactive than H.
• At the anode, OH⁻ is preferentially discharged because no halide ions are present.
